The very word “value” pulls you back into nineteenth-century philosophy.

Yet perfectly ordinary statisticians, economists such as G. F. Knapp, and lawyers had already discovered in the 1880s the idea of the “statistical law,” as opposed to the law of nature, which physicists are now noticing.
What fascinates me in your thought is something quite different.

You can hardly imagine how closely your picture of microphysical control and macroscopic large-scale and coarse effects reproduces the reality of a particular political relationship: the relationship between the individuals who possess power—the elite, the managers, the innermost leadership group, the “gang” that inevitably forms, and so on; I am still searching for the right word—and social and political power itself.

The disproportionate increase in power that flows to individuals once they are “clothed” with power is completely irrational. It is so difficult to explain that the simplest solution is still to declare that all power comes “from God.”
The same fantastic disproportion is present in every idea of the makros anthropos—the “great man,” humanity enlarged to a collective scale.
Have you ever looked at my book on Thomas Hobbes’s Leviathan?
Hobbes’s Leviathan is the magnus homo, the great man—the superman understood as a collective or objective power—derived from a mechanistic natural science.
If Hobbes were alive today, he would use your images of the relationship between microphysical and macrophysical processes to understand the relationship between the micro-human and the macro-human.

But from this I conclude that your images correspond to a particular social, political, and historical present in exactly the same way that Hobbes’s images corresponded to the machina machinarum, the machine of machines, of his own time.
Your macrophysics is really the macro-anthropos.
A macrocosm in the sense of human relationships, not the physical cosmos of the universe.
I do not know whether I have managed to make myself even remotely clear. These things are esoteric by their nature. But my desire to speak with you is too strong.
The enclosed essay (Three Types) need not detain you. It touches only occasionally on what I have in mind here.
More important is the Leviathan, a notorious book whose mere mention contaminates a person in many circles, which is why I am almost inclined to warn you away from it.
My dread of these regions runs deep.

On the occasion of Arnold Toynbee, the historian, being attached to the great American general staff, Ernst Jünger said that philosophers of history are now almost more important than atomic physicists.
Of course. They become more important to exactly the same degree that civil war, and the moral and historical undermining of the enemy, become stronger weapons than the atomic bomb.
The physics and technology of the bomb cannot answer the question: which human beings should it be dropped on?
Was it right to answer you in this way?
I dare to do so because I trust the great humanity I feel in your writings—the humanity that raises your great scientific mind above every truth confined to the laboratory.

Under the Geneva Protocol, the Kellogg Pact in its original meaning, and the whole pre-Jackson system of law for preventing war, “aggression” is a narrowly defined event that can be determined in a simple way—ideally even automatically. It is deliberately separated from all the difficult questions about substantive responsibility for the war and about the justa causa belli, the just cause of war.
The aggressor in this sense is simply whoever crosses the border first, fires the first shot, and so on.

The governing legal idea is the same as the idea behind the protection of possession: before deciding who ultimately has the better claim to the property, the law first protects the person who actually possesses it.
In other words, the immediate question of aggression is supposed to be separated from arguments about ultimate entitlement, merits, responsibility, and the underlying causa belli.
Aggression therefore remains distinguishable from the question of whether one had a just cause for war. This is extremely important for the Nuremberg trials.
Responsibility for firing the first shot is obviously something different from responsibility for the war itself.
Jackson himself sometimes still emphasized this separation from the broader question of war guilt.
In reality, as you know, all the floodgates were opened.
I do not know when, or to what extent, this can ever be repaired.

What matters above all is to keep emphasizing that the criminalization and punishment of aggression—or aggressive war—must not be mixed together with other questions, such as atrocities and inhuman acts.
I demonstrated this with extensive material in my memorandum from the summer of 1945.
At the time I was silenced.
Today I am pleased to see W. Grewe, in the discussion Nuremberg as a Legal Question, p. 99, also emphasizing this vital need for strict distinctions.
In any case, it cannot be impossible for a lawyer to distinguish the crime of firing the first shot from the crime of being responsible for the war, or still more from the mere preparation of a war.

Nor should it be impossible to recognize the injustice involved in constantly blending those two different offences together—and then blending both of them again with the entirely different crime of inhuman acts, atrocities, and so on.
In relation to the Soviet Union, such distinctions are less than ever mere legal subtleties.

Is it not remarkable that the Hague Regulations on Land Warfare of 1907 are supposed to remain completely unchanged, despite the transformation of political, economic, social, and technical conditions, whenever this works against the defendants;

while at the same time the fundamental concepts underlying those very same Hague Regulations—such as a non-discriminatory concept of war, neutrality, state sovereignty, and the “state” as the sole subject of international law—are completely transformed or abolished whenever this, too, works against the defendants?
Is it a logically fair way of thinking?
But perhaps all of this is thought through far too systematically to be presented in an atmosphere that reacts only impressionistically.
III. On being bound by the “determinations” of the first IMT [International Military Tribunal] judgment:
The purpose is clear: to preserve the foundations of the first trial as a taboo.
To the extent that the first judgment loses the self-evident authority of the reasons on which it was based, the taboo—and this supposed “binding force”—will disappear by itself.
(Dix called my memorandum from the summer of 1945 “a seminar exercise in international law.”)
The point at which the entire logic of objective power relations became choked together with the completely subjective opinions of an individual who happened to possess power.

On the question of whether the word “state” should be used as a universal concept that applies across every historical age, Heinrich Weinstock wrote to me that it was right to resist “turning history into mush.”
“On the other hand, you will probably not succeed in abolishing the word ‘state’ as the now customary name for a ‘political association,’ whatever its structure may be.”
That phrase—“you will probably not succeed”—hit me very hard.

I found it arrogant and irritating. It gives the impression that W. feels entitled to dismiss the whole point of the dispute from some lofty position. He fails to see that we are not dependent on the word “state” in order to have the general term we need.
I never said that general concepts which remove things from their historical setting are impossible or always illegitimate. That would simply be another false generalization.

I say only that such generalizations, though possible, legitimate, and necessary, belong to particular historical periods, and that a word is capable of becoming a valid universal term only within a specific age. For the word “state,” that age is over.
What was the secret—the arcanum—of the word “state”?
With ratio status: reason of state.

All the qualities of the impartial third party—or, in Hegelian language, of objective reason—that were historically connected with the state during this period disappeared once the totality of the state could become an instrument of the totality of a party. And once that happened, the word also lost its logical capacity to serve as a genuine universal concept.
Infinitely important, Gregory the Great, quoted by G. Krauss:
“It must be understood that Satan’s will is always unjust, but his power is never unjust, because his will comes from himself, while his power comes from the Lord.”
So even Satan’s power, as power, comes from God and is not evil.
How did Burckhardt arrive at the opposite thesis?
The “will to power” would then be the good will!
Yes—provided it is divine power and the will submits itself to it.
There is only one evil will: the will to powerlessness. That is: the refusal to carry out what must be carried out.
